svg.title: IS-IS specifics that matter in design: NET addressing, levels, wide metrics, and the four traps
svg.desc: Left panel explains the NET, the network entity title that names an IS-IS router: the area identifier, the system identifier which is normally derived from the loopback or MAC address, and the N-selector which is always zero. A second block explains levels: level-1 is intra-area, level-2 is the backbone, a level-1-2 router is the boundary, and the attached bit is how level-1 routers learn they can leave the area. A third block explains metrics: narrow metrics cap at 63 per link and 1023 in total, wide metrics use 24 bits and are required for segment routing, and all routers must agree on which one is in use. A right panel lists four traps: a duplicate system ID on two routers silently breaks the database; mismatched level configuration stops adjacency with no obvious error; metric style mismatch prevents wide metric advertisement; and the overload bit is used to keep traffic away from a router during a maintenance window, so seeing it set is not automatically a fault.
svg.text: IS-IS in four objects: the NET, the level, the LSP and the metric style
Every IS-IS troubleshooting session reduces to one of these four — learn them as objects, not as commands
THE NET — WHAT NAMES A ROUTER
area ID
system ID (from loopback)
N-selector, always 00
49 · 0001 · 1921.6800.1001 · 00 — one string, read left to right: area, identity, service.
LEVELS
Level 1 — intra-area
Knows only its own area. Reaches
everything else through the nearest L1-2.
Level 2 — backbone
The contiguous backbone. It must
stay connected without a separate area.
The attached bit is how a level-1 router learns “there is a way out of here”, and it is what installs the default route.
METRICS
Narrow: 6 bits per link (max 63), 10 bits path total (max 1023). Historic, still the default on some platforms.
Wide: 24 bits, needed for traffic engineering and segment routing — and every router must agree which style is in use.
FOUR TRAPS THAT LOOK LIKE PROTOCOL BUGS
1. Duplicate system ID
Two routers sharing a system ID produce one corrupt
database. The symptom is a missing router in the SPF tree.
2. Level mismatch
One side level-1, the other level-2: no adjacency, and
often no error that points at the level.
3. Metric style mismatch
Wide metric configured on one side only: the adjacency
comes up, but the cost is not what either side expects.
4. The overload bit
Set on purpose during maintenance to steer traffic away.
Seeing it set is not automatically a fault — check the change record.
What IS-IS buys you: because it runs directly on layer 2, it keeps working while IP is being repaired — the adjacency never went down,
so convergence does not stack on top of an IP failure. That property, not the TLV design, is why transport networks standardised on it.
Acceptance check: record the NET, the level and the metric style for every router in the design document, then verify them from the device. These three values
are configuration, not negotiation — nothing will correct a mismatch for you.
